q: What does a Czech importer's CBAM authority mean for an Indian supplier?
title: Czech importers: CBAM authority
short: Czechia lists two CBAM authorities: the Customs Administration and the Ministry of the Environment, each with its own contact address. A Czech importer above 50 tonnes a year needs authorised declarant status and will ask Indian suppliers for verified emissions per installation.
audience: Indian exporters of steel, aluminium, cement and fertiliser selling to buyers in Czechia, and the buyers' purchasing teams

ul: Customs and the environment ministry share the role, with separate CBAM email addresses.
Each body has its own office address in Prague.
The declaration itself goes through the EU CBAM Registry, as in every member state.

sections.h: What your buyer will ask you for
ul: The installation that made the goods and the calendar year of production.
Specific embedded emissions per tonne, with a verification report from an EU-accredited verifier if actual data is used.
The data for the free allocation adjustment and, where one applies, the carbon price paid in India.

sections.h: If you cannot send verified data
p: Your buyer can still declare using the Commission's default values, which carry a mark-up and usually cost more. A Czech buyer facing that bill will push for your actual figures or compare you with suppliers who have them.

senseible: Senseible keeps supplier invoices and the emissions data that comes with them in one dated, fingerprinted record per shipment, and its CBAM cost calculator estimates certificate cost from 2026 to 2034. Senseible does not verify emissions, register declarants or file CBAM declarations.
